46e1cfef90.q: What do lenders look for first when a business owner requests capital funding?
46e1cfef90.a: Lenders first examine the liquidity and asset position of the business. They evaluate different kinds of assets—cash, investments in the stock market that can be accessed within a week, and longer-term assets like equipment, land, or buildings. The primary consideration is how much cash can be generated from these assets or how much cash flow they will create. Lenders also assess whether the business can demonstrate productive use of capital and financial health through clean books, strong cash flow, predictable revenue, and strong management.

bd88b38d9a.q: What is the difference between productive credit and destructive credit for businesses?
bd88b38d9a.a: Productive credit is used to acquire assets or expand capacity that will generate additional revenue and cash flow—for example, an HVAC company borrowing to purchase another truck to handle a 25% margin business. Destructive or financial credit is used merely to sustain cash flow and keep an unhealthy business alive. The key distinction is whether the debt is expanding your ability to make money or just keeping you afloat. Productive credit expands productivity and capacity, while destructive credit is consumer-style debt used to manage cash flow without generating new productive capacity.

bdc90ffd2f.a: Banks require businesses to position themselves with the right financial ratios, which can be found by researching SBA requirements and typical banking standards such as Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR). The positioning involves ensuring clean books, proper P&L structure with correct categorization below the net profit line, and appropriate entity structure—whether LLC, S-Corp, or C-Corp—as different entities have different accounting rules for assets, liabilities, and income categorization. bab9787b2d.q: Why should businesses build financial health and capital access relationships before they need funding?
bab9787b2d.a: Capital access and positioning must be built before you need it because playing catch-up when an opportunity arrives is frustrating and constrains your options. If you wait until an opportunity shows up to build fundability, you're left hoping to be liquid enough to act. For businesses preparing for acquisition or sale, waiting until the last moment means missing out on significant value—what could be achieved easily with a year of preparation requires a much more painful process if done in just weeks.
